Source: http://www.canoe.ca/LondonFreePress/home.html

Posted June 8, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: This is a good piece, but both its errors and its arguments make the clear the need for a nationwide Canadian organization to oppose marijuana prohibition. Amazingly, although there are some outstanding Canadian activists, Canada has moved much closer to ending marijuana prohibition than most countries without having an effective national organization advancing the cause.

There are two general consequences of this.

First, even friendly commentators and newspapers sometimes commit errors of fact much more serious than those in this column.


See
Canada’s National Paper Falls For the Party Line
and
Canada’s National Post Parrots UN Prohibitionist Propaganda In Two Shameful Articles
and
Even The Ottawa Citizen Can Fall For Prohibitionist Propaganda,
But This Is A Good Overview Of The Canadian Border Situation.
Look Out For The New Cameras!

This happens in part because there is no Canadian equivalent of DEAland’s NORML to which Canadian journalists can turn for fact checking. I know from personal experience that some papers will ignore the facts to fit their story’s predetermined conclusions, but Canadian papers are generally much less likely to do that than DEAland papers.
See
The Racist Origins Of Canada’s Marijuana Prohibition Reported In the National Post.

For that reason, a Canadian NORML could be even more effective than DEAland NORML.

Second, because there is no organization devoted to keeping the issue on the public agenda, as the author says, " It's difficult enough to find a champion for the medicinal use of marijuana, let alone recreational use. " Actually, it is not that difficult to find lots of people making the case for medical marijuana, but we need to make it easier for Canadian journalists – and other opinion leaders -- to find everything they need to know about marijuana and marijuana prohibition in Canada.

Canada NORML was originally founded by John Conroy, the well-known B. C. criminal defense lawyer, who represents Rene Boje as well as the Vancouver Compassion Club. He was also the counsel in the recent B. C. challenge to the marijuana laws.
See

British Columbia Court Rules Two to One That Marijuana Possession Laws Must Be Decided By Parliament. Dissent Makes Hearing By Supreme Court Likely. Facts Make Marijuana Prohibition Look Bad, Again.

Over the last few years, Canada NORML has been moribund, but now Conroy is again the organization president, and there will be a concerted effort to revive it, and make it the source of information on Canadian marijuana issues.

The job here will certainly be much easier than in DEAland where marijuana prohibition is the state ideology to which all else, including the Constitution is now subordinated.

Although there are some die-hard Canadian prohibitionists, notably Ontario Premier Mike Harris, who has reiterated his opposition even to decriminalization,

See
The Reality Of the Marijuana Situation In Canada: Unequal Injustice.
Alcohol Costs Canadian Health Almost 100 Times As Much As Marijuana.
Tobacco: Almost 200 As Much – Article and Editorial
and
Major Canadian Papers Carry Op-eds And Editorial Against Marijuana Prohibition.
-- 3 Excellent Examples.
there is no Canadian equivalent to the massive government subsidized prohibitionist propaganda organizations that dominate the public discourse in DEAland. In fact, only the police, notably the Mounties and the local narks, really support marijuana prohibition.
See
Canadian Paper Gives Mounties Free Ride On Prohibitionist Propaganda
On Marijuana Growing; Lying At The Public Expense

Oh well, then there are the Alberta papers.
See
Article From The Calgary Sun Is So Dumb That Reading It Could Cause Brain Damage.
Prohibitionist Drivel At Its Worst.
and
More Prohibitionist Nonsense From Edmonton About Indoor Growing; RCMP Targets Property And Assets

On the other hand, there is the usual political inertia, and there is no one focusing on the need to end marijuana prohibition. The real problem is not so much to win the arguments. We really won a long time ago, but we have instead to insist on the importance of the issue and to keep it on the public agenda. That is where Canada NORML comes in.)


See
Ottawa Citizen Practices First Class Journalism
A Brilliantly Insightful Editorial: " Marijuana isn’t just a serious issue. It’s huge. "

June 7, 2000
From The London Free Press
letters@lfpress.com
http://www.canoe.ca/LondonFreePress/home.html
http://www.lfpress.com/londoncalling/SelectForum.asp
By Hartley Steward

NEW NATIONAL POLICY ON DRUGS OVERDUE

Julian Fantino's Right: Canada Should Decriminalize Marijuana
See
Toronto Police Chief Supports Decrim -- At the Option of The Narks – And " Education Or Treatment Programs " For Marijuana Users. The Therapeutic Police State. -- 2 Articles

How overdue is the legalization of marijuana? Toronto's loquacious police chief, Julian Fantino, recently called for a degree of decriminalization of the wacky weed and no one has batted an eye. Attitudes to marijuana use have come a long way in the last decade.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice the confusion of the terms " decriminalization " and " legalization. " Fantino made very clear that he is opposed to " legalization, " and he is not actually in favor of real " decriminalization " but rather a formalization of the current practice under which the police let some people go free, while others go to jail.)

That the police chief of Canada's largest city can suggest that not everyone who smokes grass ought to be locked away in the slammer, without causing hysteria, is an indication of just how far.

" I don't think every case involving a minute amount of marijuana needs to go through the criminal justice system, " the chief said last week.

Fantino had more to say, but it comes down to the fact he doesn't think a little grass is a big thing. He'd like his police force to turn pot heads over to the health system and get on with the job of catching some really bad guys.
(MarijuanaNews note: " Turn pot heads over to the health system "?? Exactly what is the health system supposed to do for marijuana users? And why is it acceptable to refer to marijuana users as " pot heads? " That is degrading and dehumanizing. Another task for Canada NORML.)

Even 10 years ago, a large portion of the community would have been outraged at a police chief recommending we go easy on pot heads. Fantino's remarks caused a big yawn.

I would guess that's because no one cares one way or the other. The average Canadian couldn't give a hoot how many people toke up on a regular basis; much less want them punished for it.

Over the years, marijuana has been totally demystified. No one fears it. No one associates the crazed druggie with soft drugs like marijuana and hashish.
See
Poll Shows B.C. Residents Reject DEAland Pressure To Increase Penalties on Marijuana Growing.

The term " reefer madness, " which was the title of a anti-marijuana propaganda film of the 1950s, now gets a good laugh.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, Reefer Madness was made in 1936.)

Middle-class Canadians, who most likely won't adopt the lifestyle themselves, look on its use by other as completely benign.
(MarijuanaNews note: Marijuana use – per se -- is not a " lifestyle " any more than drinking wine or taking Prozac is a " lifestyle. " It is a choice of relaxants.)

The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police several years ago recommended changes to the law that would decriminalize recreational use of the drug.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, it was last year.)
See
Canadian Police Chiefs To Support " Decriminalization " Of Marijuana.
" Government will give serious consideration to recommendation. " -- 2 Stories

Police routinely overlook possession of small amounts of grass. They still feel obliged to enforce trafficking laws, but many would like to ignore them, as well.

Fantino makes the point that police forces need to be freed to do their core job, which is the prevention of crime. He laments the resources in police forces and the courts that are eaten up in the pursuit and prosecution of small-time cannabis users.

He would like " a more contemporary " approach. Indeed, given his druthers, chasing down pot smokers would not be a police force priority. Most Canadians would agree with him on the issue.

Why then do we still have legislation that sends people to jail for using marijuana recreationally? How is it that patients and doctors have had to take to the courts to get permission to use the drug medicinally? Why do they still employ helicopters in British Columbia to spot fields of marijuana amongst the legal crops?

The fact of the matter is the police and the courts both realize our marijuana laws no longer reflect the wishes of most Canadians; that their enforcement is a waste of resources which could be better deployed elsewhere. The prosecution of recreational pot and hashish users would be on very few priority lists.

The case for decriminalization of recreational marijuana and hashish use is easy to make. The police are in favour of rethinking the use, possession and trafficking laws. No one believes the consequences of a few puffs of grass should be a term in prison. There would be little resistance to changes.

A new national policy on drugs is clearly overdue.

Which raises the question of why such a change is not winding its way through the legislative process as we speak? It isn't and it won't be for some time. It's difficult enough to find a champion for the medicinal use of marijuana, let alone recreational use.

However justified, legalizing the use of marijuana and hashish -- even limited decriminalization for simple possession -- is not an issue that's going to capture the imagination of any Canadian politician of any stripe.

There are precious few political points to be scored by publicly pushing for such changes.

The legislation will remain in place and the police will continue to waste time, money and personnel chasing down tokers.
